newsitem.title: USA: Clinton proposes easing muni arbitrage rebate rule.
newsitem.headline: Clinton proposes easing muni arbitrage rebate rule.

text.p: The Clinton Administration on Monday asked the U.S. Congress to adopt a variety of provisions to simplify the nation's tax code, including five provisions to ease the IRS' arbitrage rebate rules.

Currently, local governments are required to rebate to the federal government the arbitrage they earn from issuance of tax-free bonds. But issuers complain bitterly that the rebate rules are too complicated and costly for issuers and should be amended.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said at a press briefing that the Administration will ask Congress to ease some of those concerns.

"This is really welcome," said Michael Decker, an official with PSA The Bond Market Trade Association. "Overall, the tax exempt bond community should be happy with the proposals. PSA certainly will support it."

Current law exempts from rebate bonds where proceeds are spent within six months, 18 months or 24 months. Also exempt are bonds issued by a government that does not expect to issue more than $5 miilion in bonds in a calendar year.

The White House plan would create a new three-year "spendout" exception from rebate for long-term, fixed-rate governmental bonds that meet certain minimum spending requirements, according to the plan announced by Rubin.

It also would increase the limit on "reasonably expected bond issuance" for small issuers from $5 million to $10 million, in a proposal expected to cost the federal government $59 million from 1997 to 2002, the White House said.
Under current law, no rebate is required if gross proceeds of a bond issue are spent within six months after bonds are issued.

For governmental bonds and 501(c)(3) bonds, the six month expenditure test is met if all but five percent of proceeds or $100,000, whichever is less, is spent within six months and the remaining "de minimis" amount is spent in the next six months.
Clinton's plan would define the de minimis amount as five percent of proceeds, in what is estimated to cost the U.S. $9 million between now and 2002.

Currently, rebate requirements are met if proceeds from governmental or 501(c)(3) construction bonds are spent at minimum rates over 24 months after the bonds are issued. The issuer also can elect to make a penalty payment in lieu of rebate on unspent proceeds.
This exception does not apply to proceeds invested after the 24 months as part of a bona fide debt service fund, reserve fund or certain sinking funds.
Clinton would exempt earnings on proceeds invested in bona fide debt service funds from rebate or penalty after the 24 months if "spending requirements are otherwise satisfied."
The plan is expected to cost Treasury $2 million.
Current law limits the amount of proceeds of private activity bonds that can be invested at a higher yield at any time during a bond year to 150 percent of the debt service.
Clinton would eliminate the requirement that investments be yield-restricted, but would continue to subject any arbitrage earnings to rebate, according to the plan.
Clinton's plan also would repeal expired arbitrage rebate provisions for student loan bonds.
